en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question on Inference.
1. The Question of the Non-Arising of Two Buddhas “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:

‘It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in one world-system; such a thing cannot occur.’”
And all Tathāgatas, venerable Nāgasena, teach the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment when teaching;
they speak of the four noble truths when speaking; they train in the three trainings when training;
and they instruct in the practice of heedfulness when instructing.

"If, venerable Nāgasena, the teaching of all Tathāgatas is one, their discourse is one, their training is one, and their instruction is one, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise simultaneously?
By the arising of even a single Buddha, this world becomes filled with light;
if there were a second Buddha, by the radiance of both, this world would become even more filled with light. And as for two Tathāgatas giving exhortation..."
“They would advise with ease, and they would instruct with ease; tell me the reason for this, so that I may become free from doubt.
“Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha; it is the merit of a single Tathāgata alone.”

It sustains it; for if a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him—it would shake, tremble, reel, sink, incline, crumble, scatter, blow away, and fall apart, and it would not remain in its place.
Great King, it is just as if there were a boat capable of carrying only one person: when one person has boarded, that boat would be on the verge of capsizing.

“Then, suppose a second person were to come along, similar in life-span, complexion, age, stature, and in every limb and member—neither thin nor stout—and he were to board that same ship. Would that ship, O Great King, be able to support both of them? “No indeed, Bhante;
it would move, shake, lean, incline, bend, scatter, be dispersed, and be destroyed; it would not remain steady, but would sink into the water.
“In the very same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the support for only one Buddha; it belongs to only one Tathāgata.”
It bears this quality: if a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him;
it would shake, tremble, reel, incline, lean, scatter, blow away, and fall apart, and it would not remain stable.
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to eat his fill of food until his throat was completely full.

“Suppose, great king, that man whose stomach was previously empty, full, without gaps, and made solid—having become like a staff that cannot bend—were to eat again exactly the same amount of food. Would that man, great king, be happy?
“Certainly not, venerable sir; he would die from eating it just once.”
“In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the single retainer for a Buddha; it sustains the qualities of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain them;
it would shake, tremble, quake, incline, lean, bend, scatter, dissolve, and be utterly destroyed.”
“...would it reach its destination?
“But, venerable Nāgasena, does the earth tremble from the excessive weight of the Dhamma?
“In this case, great king, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to their very rims; from one of those carts...”
“Suppose they were to take that jewel and pour it into a single cart; would that cart, Great King, be able to support the weight of the jewels from even two carts?
“No indeed, venerable sir. Its nave would burst, its spokes would break, its rim would give way, and its axle would snap.”
“Great King, does a cart break because of the excessive weight of its precious cargo?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Great King, the earth quakes because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma.”
Moreover, Great King, this reason has been set forth to illustrate the power of the Buddhas.
Listen now to another fitting reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously:
if, Great King, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at one and the same moment, a dispute would arise within their assemblies.
‘The Buddha is yours, the Buddha is ours’— thus they would become divided into two factions, just as, Great King,
a dispute might arise between the retinues of two powerful ministers, saying, ‘He is your minister,
he is our minister,’ and thus they become divided into two factions.

In the same way, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise simultaneously, a dispute would arise within their assemblies, saying, "The Buddha belongs to you" and "The Buddha belongs to us," and they would become divided into two factions.
This, Great King, is one reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
Listen further, Great King, to another reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
If, Great King, two perfectly enlightened Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, then the statement “the Buddha is the foremost” would be false;

the statement “the Buddha is the eldest” would be false; [and likewise] the statements “the Buddha is the best,” “the Buddha is distinguished,” “the Buddha is supreme,” “the Buddha is excellent,” and “the Buddha is peerless” would be false.
“If the statement that ‘the Buddha is unequaled,’ ‘the Buddha is peerless,’ ‘the Buddha is without counterpart,’ and ‘the Buddha is without rival’ were false,
then this reason, O Great King, you should accept in its true sense: that for which two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously.”
Moreover, Great King, it is the natural disposition of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world at a time.
For what reason?
Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha.
Furthermore, Great King, whatever is great in the world is but one.
The earth, Great King, is great, yet it is only one.
The ocean is great, yet it is only one.
Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, yet it is only one.
Space is great, yet it is only one.
Sakka is great, yet he is only one.
Māra is great, but he is only one.
Mahābrahmā is great, but he is only one.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is great, and he alone is such in the world.
“Wherever they arise, there is no room for another; therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises alone in the world.
“Very well explained, venerable Nāgasena, is this question by means of similes and reasons.
Even an unskilled person would be satisfied upon hearing this, how much more so one of great wisdom such as myself!”
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! This is so; thus do I accept it.
This was the first question concerning the non-arising of two Buddhas simultaneously.
